newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy coalition moves to smooth rift over Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italy coalition moves to smooth rift over Albania.

text.p: The government on Thursday moved to smooth over a potentially damaging rift between it and hardline communist allies over Italy's plans to lead a multinational security force into Albania.

The differences over the mission, which could begin late next week, mark the first time in 11 months of centre-left government that the Communist Refoundation party has so openly dissented on an important issue of foreign policy.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi has secured assent for the 5,000-strong force, up to half of it Italian, from the main centre-right opposition but not from Refoundation, on whose backing he depends for his parliamentary majority.
Given the declared centre-right stance, Refoundation cannot scupper the mission and party leader Fausto Bertinotti says he will not bring Prodi down over the issue.
But the rift hardened speculation that Prodi's fractious partnership with Refoundation is becoming unsustainable.
Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni said he found Refoundation's position "incomprehensible" but added that there was room for debate and he did not see any real threat.

"There are no alternatives to this coalition," he said. "If there is a government crisis, we will have early elections pure and simple...For that reason, I do not think there will be a crisis in the coalition."
The Senate (upper house) holds a formal vote next Tuesday, followed on Wednesday by the Chamber of Deputies.
Aides to Prodi acknowledged on Thursday that the divisions on Albania could have a knock-on effect on the domestic front as well as undermine Italy's credibility abroad.

Prodi's cabinet secretary, Enrico Micheli, however, said efforts to swing Refoundation behind the force would be made in the coming days. "The (Senate) vote is on Tuesday. That leaves us a plenty of time to reason," he told reporters.
Political sources said Micheli and Junior Foreign Minister Piero Fassino met Bertinotti later on Thursday.

Refoundation has proved a difficult partner for Prodi since he took office last May, primarily in its stiff resistance to his drive to rein in public spending in order to qualify Italy for Europe's planned single currency.
Bertinotti said on Thursday that if he did decide to withdraw his backing for Prodi, thus bringing the government down, it would be over economics and not Albania.

His party's stance has angered forces inside Prodi's coalition as Italian soldiers prepare to embark on a mission fraught with potential dangers from lawless mafias and uncontrolled gunmen in anarchic Albania.
The opposition Freedom Alliance, while professing backing for the force "in the national interest", has meanwhile sought to exploit the disarray in Prodi's ranks.
"If Prodi had an ounce of dignity he would acknowledge that he no longer has a majority," said Gianfranco Fini, whose hard-right National Alliance is part of the bloc.

The force will secure ports, airports and transport routes for a planned international relief mission to Albania, where a revolt sparked by the collapse of shady investment schemes has put rebel committees in control of southern towns.
Bertinotti's opposition stems from what he says are unacceptable risks to Italian troops after the sinking last week of a refugee boat in collision with a navy ship.
He has also argued that the force could shore up Albania's rightist President Sali Berisha, whose resignation is a key demand of southern Albanian rebels.
